rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3-4 - authors run their own distributed Tetis model (100 Monte Carlo runs, 1994-2015) with multi-objective calibration against observed evaporative index, groundwater levels in four wells and soil moisture. Q2: Section 4.2 / Figure 6 - mean annual recharge for flood irrigation (231 mm) exceeded drip irrigation (210 mm) by ~21 mm (10%); flood recharge higher in 16 of 20 years; model output checked against observed groundwater levels (Figure 4) and evaporative index (Figure 3) from the real system. Q4: Section 4.1 Figure 5 and Section 4.2/5.1 - model simulates soil water storage in wet and dry parts and ETa; authors attribute lower drip recharge during rainfall to the model's lower soil storage potential under drip (flood-irrigated areas could accommodate on average 35% more precipitation on the day of rainfall) and to flood return flows outside rainy days (Figure 8). Q6: Section 2 and 3.3.3 - results are for a 913 km2 study area with 382 km2 irrigated land across 68 irrigation sectors, aggregated at basin/regional scale. Q8: Section 5.3 - no split-sample validation possible, which increases uncertainty of absolute recharge values; soil moisture data not measured inside modeled area; Section 5.2 - pixel splitting limits interpretation to sector scale and is a strong simplification; Section 6 - findings limited to the Mediterranean region. Q9: Figures 6-8 - results reported as boxplots and min/max/median across the 12 accepted model parameterizations, propagating parameter uncertainty to the recharge estimates; Table 2 reports standard errors of regression coefficients.
rows.notes: Q3 no: single modeling approach; multi-variable calibration does not constitute an independent second method for estimating recharge difference. Q5 no: one region, one crop type (citrus orchards). Q7 doubtful: authors report that flood recharge clearly exceeds drip only in below-average rainfall years and during the March-September irrigation season, with the reverse in wet years and in autumn/winter (Figure 7); this is reported as a gradient/seasonal pattern rather than stated as a requirement, so rated no. Note the study also finds precipitation has ~4x greater influence on recharge than irrigation type, and that drip can exceed flood recharge in wet years, which qualifies the claim.

notes: Full text available; modeling study calibrated against field observations (evaporative index, groundwater levels, soil moisture) in the Plana de Valencia Sur, Spain. Supporting information not included.
